Those are the moments that create friction. Because now you’re not choosing between good and bad. You’re choosing between good and slightly better. And the more I think about it, the more I believe we’re focusing on the wrong part of that statement. Most conversations about AI seem to revolve around what it can create. Can it design a screen? Can it write code? Can it generate a user flow? Can it summarize research? Can it produce a strategy deck? The answer, increasingly, is yes. And not only can it do those things, it can often do them surprisingly well. What I think we talk about less is what happens after AI has generated all those ideas. Because that’s where I’ve started noticing the real shift. Not in generation. In judgment. A Small Design Review That Stuck With Me This realization didn’t come from some grand AI transformation project. It came from a fairly normal design conversation. I was reviewing a design recommendation that had originally been generated with the help of AI. The recommendation itself wasn’t bad. Honestly, if someone had shown it to me without mentioning AI, I probably would have described it as a sensible solution. It solved the problem. It followed familiar patterns. It had a logical structure. There was nothing obviously wrong with it. But as we discussed it as a team, something interesting happened. The deeper we got into the realities of the users, the more apparent it became that another option would probably work better. Not because the original concept was flawed. Not because AI had missed some critical piece of information. Simply because real people are messy. And products live in the messy world, not in the logical one. That distinction has been stuck in my head ever since. Earlier in My Career, Ideas Were Expensive When I first started designing, coming up with multiple viable solutions took real effort. You’d sketch > You’d whiteboard > You’d debate> You’d throw half your concepts away. You’d spend days or weeks exploring directions before you felt comfortable presenting a recommendation. There was value in that process because generating ideas was genuinely hard. That’s no longer true. Today I can ask AI for ten navigation patterns, ten dashboard layouts, ten onboarding concepts, or ten feature ideas and receive a collection of reasonable answers almost instantly. Sometimes I’ll generate a handful of concepts before my morning coffee is even finished brewing. That’s incredible. But it also means the scarcity has changed. When something becomes abundant, it stops being the thing that differentiates you. Twenty years ago, producing ten ideas was impressive. Today, everybody can produce ten ideas. Tomorrow, everybody might produce a hundred. The Problem Isn’t Bad Ideas The more I use AI, the more convinced I become that bad ideas aren’t the problem. In fact, bad ideas are easy. Nobody struggles to reject a terrible suggestion. If AI recommends something absurd, the decision is straightforward. The genuinely difficult situations are when AI suggests something that’s actually quite good . Those are the moments that create friction. Because now you’re not choosing between good and bad. You’re choosing between good and slightly better. You’re choosing between multiple reasonable directions. You’re evaluating trade-offs. And trade-offs are where experience starts to matter . I think that’s why I find myself valuing judgment more every month I work with AI. The tool keeps getting better at generating possibilities. My responsibility shifts toward deciding which possibilities deserve to become reality. Users Have Never Behaved Like Designers Imagine One of the most humbling lessons in UX is discovering how products are actually used. As designers, product managers, and engineers, we often review experiences under ideal conditions. We sit quietly > We focus > We examine every detail > We carefully compare alternatives > We pay attention. Users don’t. Not because they’re careless. Because they’re busy. They’re checking a dashboard between meetings. They’re trying to submit an expense report before school pickup. They’re looking at their phone while walking through an airport. They’re multitasking during a Teams call. They’re juggling life while trying to complete a task. Over the years, I’ve seen incredibly sophisticated solutions lose to simpler ones because the simpler option required less thinking. I’ve seen powerful features go unused because they weren’t immediately obvious. I’ve seen teams spend months perfecting functionality that users barely noticed. And I’ve seen small UX changes dramatically improve an experience because they aligned with how people actually behave rather than how we hoped they would behave. That gap between theory and reality is where judgment lives. AI Is Very Good at Logic. Design Is About Consequences. This is where I think things get interesting.
